query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially homogeneous single‐phase high–entropy alloy, service‐relevant thermal exposure and mechanical loading induce subtle local chemical reordering at grain boundaries that lowers their cohesion, thereby initiating brittle intergranular fracture even in the absence of gross precipitation or conventional segregation seen in simpler alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single–phase, compositionally complex HEA (e.g., a CoCrFeMnNi–type alloy) with uniformly distributed elements and ductile grain interiors.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to prolonged thermal aging at a service–relevant temperature (well below any phase transformation threshold) combined with cyclic mechanical loading designed to mimic service conditions.
generation.conditions: Temperatures and strain rates relevant to demanding engineering applications (moderate to high temperatures without inducing global phase separation), under which the alloy remains macroscopically single–phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Subtle local chemical short–range ordering at grain boundaries that creates regions of lower cohesion and inhibits dislocation transfer, leading to stress concentration.
generation.mechanism: The applied thermal and mechanical loads promote atomic rearrangements at the grain boundaries in a complex alloy; although the overall phase remains single, local enrichment or depletion of specific elements occurs. This local ordering raises the effective barrier for plastic deformation at the boundaries, making them prone to brittle failure under high strain, unlike the ductile behavior observed in the as–cast state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, thermally aged and cyclically loaded specimens will exhibit a discernible drop in ductility (e.g., lower fracture strain and toughness) and a transition towards intergranular fracture morphology under tensile testing, even though no obvious secondary phases or precipitates are detected.
generation.baseline: Initially ductile, single–phase HEA with uniform elemental distribution and high toughness under standard mechanical tests.
generation.boundary: This brittleness degradation mechanism is expected to manifest under moderate service temperatures and strain rates that allow sufficient time for boundary reordering; under extreme conditions that trigger conventional precipitation or gross segregation, different embrittlement pathways may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The rate and extent of grain boundary chemical reordering and the resulting quantitative impact on ductility remain uncertain and may vary with exact composition and service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical, as–cast HEA specimens. Expose one set to prolonged aging at a service–relevant temperature combined with cyclic loading to simulate operational stresses, while keeping the control set in the as–cast condition. After treatment, perform tensile tests and detailed fracture surface analysis (e.g., scanning electron microscopy and atom probe tomography) to assess ductility and detect any grain boundary compositional changes.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (identification of intergranular versus transgranular fracture)
Grain boundary chemical profiles (using high–resolution microscopy/atom probe analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show a statistically significant decrease in ductility or exhibit fracture modes similar to the as–cast control, and no evidence of local chemical reordering at grain boundaries is found, then the hypothesis that local boundary reordering is responsible for brittle behavior in these HEAs would be falsified.

Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. Dislocations and deformation microstructure in a B2-ordered Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are multicomponent metallic materials currently attracting high research interest. They display a unique combination of chemical disorder and crystalline long-range order, and due to their attractive properties are promising candidates for technological application. Many high-entropy alloys possess surprisingly high strength, occasionally in combination with high ductility and low density. The mechanisms effecting these attractive mechanical properties are not understood. This study addresses the deformation mechanism of a Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy, which is a two-phase material, consisting of a B2-ordered matrix and disordered body-centred inclusions. We quantitatively analyse the microstructure and dislocations in deformed samples by transmission-electron-microscopic methods including weak-beam imaging and convergent-beam electron diffraction. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
